questions.q: The three levels of biodiversity are:
questions.solution:
**Genetic diversity** — variation within a species, as in the 50,000 genetically distinct strains of rice in India.

**Species diversity** — the variety of species in a region.

**Ecosystem diversity** — the variety of habitats, from rainforest to desert to estuary.

Genetic diversity is the one most often overlooked, and it is the raw material on which natural selection acts. A species reduced to a single genetic strain is far more vulnerable, however many individuals remain.

questions.q: The species-area relationship is described by:
questions.solution:
Alexander von Humboldt's relationship is $S = CA^{Z}$, usually plotted in logarithms as $\mathbf{\log S = \log C + Z\log A}$ — a straight line of slope $Z$.

The slope $Z$ is remarkably consistent: about **0.1 to 0.2** for small regions, whatever the taxonomic group or continent.

For very large areas such as whole continents the slope is steeper, $0.6$ to $1.2$, because those areas span entirely different biomes rather than more of the same.

questions.q: The main cause of biodiversity loss is:
questions.solution:
**Habitat loss and fragmentation** is the single largest cause.

The four together are known as **The Evil Quartet**: habitat loss and fragmentation, over-exploitation, alien species invasion, and co-extinctions.

Fragmentation matters as much as outright loss: species needing large territories, and migratory animals, are badly affected even when the total remaining area looks adequate, because they cannot use it as separated patches.

questions.q: National parks and wildlife sanctuaries are examples of:
questions.solution:
**In situ** conservation protects the species **in its natural habitat** — national parks, sanctuaries, biosphere reserves, sacred groves.

It is generally preferred, because it conserves the whole ecosystem and the species continues to evolve in its natural setting.

**Ex situ** conservation removes the organism to a protected setting — zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks, cryopreservation. It is the fallback when the habitat cannot be saved, or the last resort for a species too depleted to survive in the wild.

Species diversity **decreases from the equator towards the poles**.

Three explanations are usually offered: tropical latitudes have been **undisturbed for far longer**, since temperate regions were glaciated repeatedly; the tropical environment is **less seasonal and more constant**, favouring niche specialisation; and there is **more available solar energy**, supporting greater productivity.

The Amazon rainforest alone holds well over 40,000 plant species.

questions.q: The current loss of species is often called the sixth extinction because:
options: Six species go extinct each year
It is the sixth mass extinction in Earth's history
questions.solution:
Five mass extinctions have occurred in the geological past, the best known being the end-Cretaceous event that removed the dinosaurs.

The present loss is called the **sixth** because its rate is comparable to those events — currently estimated at **100 to 1000 times** the natural background rate.

The difference is the cause. The previous five were driven by asteroid impacts, volcanism and climate shifts. This one has a **single species** as its cause, which is also the reason it is the first that could in principle be stopped.

questions.q: A biodiversity hotspot is a region with:
options: High species richness, many endemics, and serious threat
questions.solution:
A hotspot must satisfy **two** criteria together: exceptional **endemism** — species found nowhere else — and serious **threat**, having lost at least $70\%$ of its original habitat.

Both are required. High diversity alone does not make a hotspot; the threat is what makes it urgent.

India has four: the **Western Ghats and Sri Lanka**, the **Himalaya**, the **Indo-Burma** region and **Sundaland**. Hotspots cover a very small share of the land surface yet hold a large fraction of all species, which is what makes them efficient conservation targets.

questions.q: Paul Ehrlich's rivet popper hypothesis compares an ecosystem to:
options: An aeroplane held together by rivets, each rivet a species
questions.solution:
Ehrlich likened an ecosystem to an **aeroplane** held together by thousands of **rivets**, each rivet a species.

Losing a few rivets may weaken the plane without causing failure. But rivets continue to be lost, and at some point the loss becomes **catastrophic** — and there is no way to know in advance which rivet is the critical one.

The analogy makes a further point: rivets on the **wings** matter far more than those on the seats. Losing a **keystone species** is far more dangerous than losing a rare one with few connections.

questions.q: The Earth Summit that produced the Convention on Biological Diversity was held in:
questions.solution:
The **Earth Summit** was held in **Rio de Janeiro in 1992**, and produced the Convention on Biological Diversity.

The follow-up World Summit on Sustainable Development was at Johannesburg in 2002, where 190 countries pledged to reduce the rate of biodiversity loss by 2010.

Kyoto (1997) and Paris (2015) concern climate change rather than biodiversity.

questions.q: For the species-area relationship on a logarithmic scale within a small region, what is the typical value of the slope $Z$? Give the midpoint of the usual range.
questions.solution:
For small regions the slope $Z$ lies in the range **0.1 to 0.2**, so the midpoint is about $\mathbf{0.15}$.

The striking finding is how **constant** it is — the same range emerges whatever the taxonomic group and whatever the continent, for plants, birds, molluscs and bats alike.

For very large areas such as entire continents it rises to $0.6$ to $1.2$, because those areas encompass wholly different biomes.

questions.q: Approximately how many biodiversity hotspots are recognised worldwide?
questions.solution:
About $\mathbf{34}$ hotspots are usually cited, though the number has risen to 36 as more regions qualify.

Together they cover a little over $2\%$ of the Earth's land surface yet hold a very large share of all endemic species — which is precisely what makes them such efficient targets for limited conservation funding.

questions.q: Approximately what percentage of the world's recorded species does India hold, despite having only about $2.4\%$ of the land area?
questions.solution:
India holds roughly $\mathbf{8\%}$ of the world's recorded species on about $2.4\%$ of the land area — over three times its share.

This is why India is classed as one of the world's **megadiverse** countries.

questions.q: How many mass extinctions had occurred in Earth's history before the present one?
questions.solution:
$\mathbf{5}$ mass extinctions, which is why the current loss is termed the **sixth extinction**.

The most recent of the five was the end-Cretaceous event about 65 million years ago, which ended the dinosaurs.

questions.q: Approximately what percentage of all described species are insects?
questions.solution:
Insects make up roughly $\mathbf{70\%}$ of all described species — more than **20 out of every 25** animal species.

The biologist J.B.S. Haldane is said to have remarked that the Creator, if one exists, must have an inordinate fondness for beetles.

questions.q: Describe the patterns of biodiversity and the causes of its loss. Compare in situ and ex situ conservation, explaining the circumstances in which each is appropriate, and give reasons why biodiversity should be conserved.
questions.solution:
**Patterns of biodiversity.**

**The latitudinal gradient.** Diversity falls from the equator towards the poles. Colombia, near the equator, has about 1400 bird species; New York at $41^\circ$N has 105; Greenland at $71^\circ$N has 56. Three reasons are usually given: tropical regions have remained **undisturbed for far longer**, since temperate regions were repeatedly glaciated; the tropical environment is **less seasonal and more constant**, which favours niche specialisation; and **more solar energy** is available, supporting higher productivity.

**The species-area relationship.** Within a region, species richness rises with area as $S = CA^{Z}$, a straight line of slope $Z$ on log axes. The slope is remarkably constant at $0.1$ to $0.2$ regardless of taxon or continent.

**Causes of loss: the Evil Quartet.**

**1. Habitat loss and fragmentation** — the largest single cause. The Amazon rainforest, the lungs of the planet, is being cleared for soya and cattle. Fragmentation matters independently of total loss, because animals needing large territories or migration routes cannot use scattered patches even when their combined area seems sufficient.

**2. Over-exploitation** — Steller's sea cow and the passenger pigeon were hunted to extinction, and many marine fisheries are now over-harvested.

**3. Alien species invasion** — the Nile perch introduced into Lake Victoria drove more than 200 native cichlid species to extinction. **Parthenium**, **Lantana** and water hyacinth are damaging invaders in India.

**4. Co-extinctions** — a species does not go alone. Its obligate parasites, its specialist pollinators and its mutualists go with it. In a plant-pollinator pair evolved for each other exclusively, the loss of one guarantees the loss of the other.

**In situ conservation.**

Protecting the species **in its natural habitat**: national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biosphere reserves and sacred groves.

**Advantages.** The **whole ecosystem** is conserved, not one species. It is far cheaper per species, since protecting one hotspot saves thousands at once. The species continues to **evolve and adapt** in its natural setting, keeping its genetic diversity and its behaviour intact.

**Limitations.** It needs large areas, it competes with human land use, and it cannot help a species already reduced below a viable population.

**Ex situ conservation.**

Removing the organism to a protected setting: zoos, botanical gardens, wildlife safari parks, **seed banks**, gene banks and **cryopreservation** of gametes and embryos at $-196^\circ\text{C}$.

**Advantages.** It can save a species whose habitat is already gone. Cryopreservation stores genetic material almost indefinitely in little space. Captive breeding can rebuild numbers for later reintroduction, and the black-footed ferret and California condor were both saved this way.

**Limitations.** Only a **small number of individuals** can be kept, so genetic diversity is lost and inbreeding follows. Animals may lose the behaviours needed for survival in the wild. It is expensive per species. And it conserves the organism without conserving its **ecosystem** or its ecological role.

**When each is appropriate.** In situ conservation should be the default wherever a viable habitat and population still exist. Ex situ conservation is the **emergency measure** — for a species whose habitat is destroyed, or whose numbers have fallen too low to recover unaided. In practice the two are complementary: captive breeding is only worth doing if there is somewhere to release the animals back into, which means in situ protection must continue alongside it.

**Why conserve biodiversity: three kinds of argument.**

**Narrowly utilitarian.** Humans draw direct economic benefit: food, firewood, fibre, and above all **medicine**. About 25% of drugs are derived from plants, and some 25,000 plant species are used in traditional medicines. The genetic diversity of wild crop relatives is the raw material for breeding disease resistance into cultivated varieties.

**Broadly utilitarian.** Ecosystems provide services that are not traded and are hard to replace. The Amazon produces an estimated 20% of the Earth's oxygen. Pollinators sustain the crops we eat. Ecosystems regulate climate, purify water, form soil and control floods. These services are enormous in value and become visible mainly when they fail.

**Ethical.** Every species has an intrinsic value and a right to exist, independent of its usefulness to us. We share this planet with millions of other species and have a moral obligation to pass them on to the next generation in no worse a state than we received them.

The ethical argument is the one that does not depend on our being able to name a use — which matters, because most species have never been studied well enough for anyone to know what they are good for.
